## Structure and components

- [statement] Repository retrieval needs maintained structure as well as storage: the ResearchOps Community includes taxonomies, structured vocabularies, librarianship and delivery of insights to research consumers; NN/g recommends a documented initial taxonomy that stays simple and evolves through use. (medium confidence) — https://researchops.community/blog/project/research-repositories/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/
- [statement] Harbor’s navigation-state discussion contains conflicting positions: the reporter wants page and search criteria restored on Back; one contributor defends refreshing on re-entry and suggests opening details in another tab; another proposes restoring criteria from the URL while fetching results again. The latter is a proposal, not evidence of an implemented fix. (low confidence) — https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/issues/23142 · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## How it works

- [statement] Preserve each participant’s sequence and context when analyzing entries. Examine how experiences change over time and what circumstances accompany changes; repeated observations support within-person questions as well as comparisons between participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/
- [statement] Distinguish adherence to individual prompts from retention of participants. Missing responses can occur when responding is inconvenient or unsafe, and selective reporting can bias the contexts represented. Longitudinal UX studies should plan for participant dropout as well as incomplete entries. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/
- [statement] Signal-contingent capture prompts participants to report when notified. Random or stratified-random signals can sample different moments across the day; choose timing around relevant contexts and participants’ schedules. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Onboard participants with plain instructions about what and when to report, the expected detail, tools, and incentives. Explain the importance of timely responses and train participants to recognize the target event or construct. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Observational experience sampling can examine co-occurrence, lagged associations, and temporal ordering, but these patterns alone do not establish causation because confounding is not experimentally controlled. (low confidence) — https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] The caregiver EMA study could not isolate the effects of survey length or delivery frequency because participants received the same surveys. Its low-burden findings should not be treated as experimental proof of an optimal protocol. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Burghardt recommends checking current applicability through stakeholder flags, researcher review during reuse, or targeted review of a research subset. He also cautions against discarding research solely because it is old; age and present relevance require separate judgment. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] GOV.UK recommends fully anonymised research extracts whenever possible and removing or obscuring direct identifiers, contact details and confidential information even when full anonymisation would remove useful context. Non-anonymised outputs require restricted sharing. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] Jake Burghardt proposes assessing evidence durability using collection or reporting date, research type, investigated topic, audience or market changes, and severity or priority. His example expiration rules are explicitly possibilities to adapt, not universal best practices; old research can remain applicable when its context has not changed. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] Research-data retention and insight relevance require separate judgments: GOV.UK says to establish a deletion process for unneeded data or expired retention and data without clear consent, while Burghardt describes research that satisfies governance rules but is no longer applicable to the product. Retaining data does not establish its relevance. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a
- [statement] Communicate the effect of search and filtering with result counts and distinguish waiting from completion or no results. Pencil & Paper recommends counts as feedback on narrowing; W3C identifies brief search-status messages as status updates when they neither take focus nor refresh the page. W3C explicitly excludes the result list itself from that status-message definition. (medium confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX · also: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html
- [statement] NN/G warns that moving the page while someone is selecting filters can make them lose their place or click the wrong control. It also notes that keeping the old scroll position can hide a short result list and resemble an unfinished or empty search. Decide when to reveal updated results in relation to the user’s current filtering activity. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Hearst’s search-interface evaluation chapter recommends realistic tasks and comparisons over the same document collection. It cautions that prewritten queries reduce realism for query-formulation research, although they can be acceptable when evaluating result-summary assessment. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use event-contingent capture for a clearly defined event of interest. It suits infrequent or unpredictable events, but logging every occurrence becomes burdensome when events are frequent. Give participants an unambiguous event definition. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use interval-based capture at predetermined times when periodic reporting fits the question. Check whether the selected times miss intervening events or systematically underrepresent other parts of the day. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use signal-triggered capture when participants should respond to notifications. Signals may follow random or mixed schedules; they can sample different times of day and reduce reliance on participants remembering to initiate entries. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use interval-contingent capture at predetermined times when regular reporting fits the question. Intervals that are too long can miss intervening events; intervals that are too short increase burden. A fixed reporting time can also skew which daily experiences receive detail. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use citations from planning and decision artifacts back to research, and record reuse requests and their resulting work products. These practitioner practices make research use more traceable, but citation alone does not establish that a decision was correct or that research caused a business outcome. (medium confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1 · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Keep repeated prompts short and plainly worded. Explain why timely responses matter and train participants to recognize qualifying events when the task cannot be simplified. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.rallyuxr.com/post/diary-studies-101-an-actionable-guide-for-ux-researchers
- [statement] Repeated measurement can change responses or experiences. APA identifies anticipation of fixed reports as a reactivity risk; Eisele and colleagues found changes in completion time and within-person variability in a student study, while the implications for data validity remained unresolved. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Eisele2023AMMII.pdf
- [statement] The severe-mental-disorder ESM meta-analysis found lower compliance with more evaluations per day and shorter spacing, but no significant association with study duration. These associations are population- and reporting-dependent, so they do not establish a universal UX cadence or prove that every longer study causes more attrition. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Filter application should account for intent, selection complexity and response speed. NN/G recommends interactive updates for exploration and batch application for known multi-criterion searches or slow responses; Pencil & Paper likewise distinguishes instant, per-filter and global application. Neither supports one application mode for every search task. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX · also: https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering
- [statement] Hearst’s search-interface evaluation guidance recommends realistic tasks and considers time, effort and error severity. It cautions that longer exploration can reflect a better experience, so shorter sessions alone do not establish success. Prewritten query terms can isolate result-summary assessment but reduce realism when evaluating query formulation or term suggestions. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Immediate filtering is conditional on the task and response speed. NN/g recommends interactive updates for exploration and batch application for known compound criteria or slow responses; Pencil & Paper likewise recommends a global Apply action for heavy datasets or slow applications. These are design recommendations, not a measured universal performance advantage. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX · also: https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering
- [statement] Hearst identifies task time, effort and error severity as interface evaluation measures but cautions against equating shorter sessions with better search: longer exploration and refinement can be useful. Search evaluation should interpret timing in the context of the task and participant differences. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] UX diary studies collect participants’ self-reported experiences over time in everyday contexts; experience sampling uses repeated momentary reports to examine within-person processes. These reports are sampled accounts rather than a complete behavioral record. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/
- [statement] Fixed schedules can make participation easier to plan but may change the situations participants report from. The ESM meta-analysis did not establish a universally optimal fixed-versus-random schedule and recommends choosing according to the scientific question. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] For temporal analysis, inspect observation gaps instead of treating every missing report as interchangeable: the caregiver EMA paper notes that nonadherence may be nonrandom and connected to the momentary exposures under study, which can impair across-day relationship analyses. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] Set diary-study duration from the research question, behavior frequency, and the time needed for the activity to unfold; NN/g presents different reporting periods for different behaviors rather than one universal duration. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Distinguish response compliance from participant retention. In the severe-mental-disorder ESM meta-analysis, compliance measures completed versus protocol-possible evaluations, whereas retention measures participants included in final analyses; minimum-compliance exclusions can link the two. Report definitions and exclusion rules. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] A research repository is distinguished by its research contents and purpose of consumption and reuse, rather than by a particular software category: the ResearchOps Community includes knowledge bases, wikis, drives and file cabinets, while UX Mastery describes searchable, reusable UX research data. (medium confidence) — https://github.com/researchops/research_repositories · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://uxmastery.com/how-to-organize-and-reuse-research-insights/
- [statement] For evidence traceability, Zack Naylor recommends insight records containing a name, contextual description, tags and supporting notes, observations, artifacts or data. Jake Burghardt recommends insight summaries that preserve study context and link to component reports and evidence; these are practitioner patterns rather than demonstrated universal requirements. (medium confidence) — https://uxmastery.com/how-to-organize-and-reuse-research-insights/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions, https://skimle.com/blog/building-a-research-repository-that-people-actually-use
- [statement] Repository governance must accommodate deletion rather than indefinite evidence preservation: the Service Manual requires a deletion process for data no longer needed or at the end of retention, and organisation that permits finding and deleting a participant’s specific data. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] NN/g reports that missing ownership and burdensome contribution workflows are adoption problems, and recommends designated responsibility for tags and contributions. The ResearchOps Community likewise describes librarians doing data gardening and developing the research narrative. These sources support operational ownership, rather than expecting storage alone to sustain reuse. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://researchops.community/blog/project/research-repositories/
- [statement] For research-request intake, Burghardt recommends entry points including intake queues and planning templates, a rubric for self-service versus collaborative support, and explicit communication of contradictions and certainty. Existing research can clarify a request and reveal gaps; analogous findings require judgment rather than being treated as exact answers. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1 · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] In Baymard’s desktop ecommerce testing, some users treated autocomplete suggestions as editable starting points. Baymard recommends copying the keyboard-highlighted suggestion into the search field so users can refine it before submission; this is a recommendation grounded in that context, rather than a universal autocomplete rule. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/copy-search-suggestion-to-search-field · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper recommends making active filters visible outside collapsed controls and providing clearing at both individual-filter and global levels. Its advanced-filter pattern lets users add or exclude conditions and choose whether results match all, one or none; products should expose the supported composition rather than leave it implicit. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] For ecommerce zero-result recovery, Baymard recommends relevant alternative categories or simplified queries rather than search tips alone. If an alternate query is automatically applied, its recommendation includes telling users that the original query had no results and that the displayed results come from the revision. Preserve that distinction when communicating relevance. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/no-results-page · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] NN/g identifies a trade-off in batch filtering: waiting until criteria are complete avoids repeated waits, but delays feedback about available combinations and can allow a combination that produces no results. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper describes advanced filtering as composing conditions with explicit relations, including equality, ranges and and/or combinations. This guidance supports exposing compound filter logic rather than leaving users to infer how selections combine. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Choose duration from the research question, event frequency, and time needed for the activity to unfold. Choose cadence to capture the contexts and temporal changes of interest while limiting reporting burden; a standard number of diary days is not a substitute for this rationale. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Prepare clear instructions, expected reporting effort, example entries, and a contact channel. Brief participants on unfamiliar tasks or tools. Pilot the design and materials before the main study, and avoid examples that steer participants toward particular experiences. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://medium.com/somiacx/lessons-from-running-a-diary-study-e35ddd1e4060, https://www.rallyuxr.com/post/diary-studies-101-an-actionable-guide-for-ux-researchers
- [statement] High-frequency reports can reduce retrospective recall demands and reveal within-person changes, but scheduled reporting can itself influence responses. Anticipating a fixed reporting time is a possible source of reactivity. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/
- [statement] Monitor entries during collection and ask for clarification while the event is fresh. Use a post-study interview to probe ambiguous entries and reflect on the broader experience; diary screenshots or entries can serve as personalized interview prompts. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://medium.com/somiacx/lessons-from-running-a-diary-study-e35ddd1e4060
- [statement] In a meta-analysis of ESM studies concerning severe mental disorders, lower sampling frequency and longer intervals were associated with higher compliance. Study duration was not significantly associated with compliance or retention. These are population- and protocol-specific associations, not universal UX cadence thresholds. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] A caregiver EMA study found that momentary experiences and participant characteristics mattered for burden and adherence; its reported burden was low and it found no strong indicators that design attributes created persistent burden. Low adherence should therefore not automatically be interpreted as proof that a protocol is too demanding. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Pilot the protocol before the main study to test instructions, tools, survey length, prompt timing, and burden in everyday contexts; use participant feedback to revise the design. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] NN/g recommends monitoring entries during collection, asking timely clarification questions, and agreeing on a contact method and periodic reminders that do not become overly intrusive. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Plan a post-study interview grounded in each participant’s entries to clarify vague accounts, probe missing detail, and invite reflection on the broader experience. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Keep repeated surveys brief and consider participants’ daily routines. Frequent prompts can intrude on activities, and participant burden can affect both response rates and the quality of completed answers. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] Eisele and colleagues caution that their student-sample findings may not generalize to other populations. Behavioral changes were rare, effects of protocol and individual characteristics were inconsistent, and the study did not establish whether observed reactive changes damaged validity. (low confidence) — https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Eisele2023AMMII.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Analyze diary experiences in their temporal and contextual sequence. For quantitative experience-sampling data, account for repeated observations nested within people and temporal dependence; distinguish within-person associations from between-person differences. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] NN/g warns that incentive rules can distort diary data: response requirements should be realistic, and open-ended payment for extra entries can encourage manufactured interactions. Design compensation around the expected effort and natural activity. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] For government user research, the GOV.UK Service Manual says to keep consent records with the research data and make them matchable, and to reuse or share the data only for the purpose covered by that consent. This supports consent-compatible evidence links without assuming repository access grants permission for new uses. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] For research outputs, the Service Manual recommends fully anonymised extracts where possible. If an output is not fully anonymised, restrict access to people who need it and share it only with the third parties disclosed to participants. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] Display research dates and assess applicability before reuse. Burghardt proposes context-sensitive durability rules and review states; these are illustrative governance choices, not validated universal expiry periods. (medium confidence) — https://skimle.com/blog/building-a-research-repository-that-people-actually-use · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a
- [statement] For research-request intake, Burghardt proposes using intake queues and planning entry points to connect questions with existing findings, choosing self-service or researcher support by question importance, query complexity, and research literacy. He recommends making contradictions and uncertainty explicit in the answer. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1 · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] NN/g’s repository study used a practitioner survey and follow-up interviews. Its findings describe reported adoption barriers and associations; they should not be treated as an experiment proving that purchasing a repository tool improves decisions. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] Repository rollout advice differs: Zack Naylor, Aurelius co-founder writing for UX Mastery, recommends starting now; NN/g reports that organisations with low UX maturity may lack readiness and stakeholder buy-in. Treat the first position as vendor practitioner advice, not a universal adoption rule. (low confidence) — https://uxmastery.com/how-to-organize-and-reuse-research-insights/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/
- [statement] GOV.UK advises approved storage for research data, restricting access to those who specifically need it, and preventing copying or downloading where technology permits. These recommendations apply to repository source data as well as research outputs that remain identifiable. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] For revalidation, Burghardt proposes stakeholder flags, researcher reviews during reuse, targeted manual review, metadata-based automation and recurring broader review. These are alternative curation approaches with different effort requirements, not evidence that every repository needs an automated expiry policy. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] For decision traceability, Burghardt recommends links from planning artifacts to research rationale, recording resulting goals or backlog items, and keeping a register of insight pulls. His reported Amazon experience illustrates how citations connected research to later launches; he explicitly limits that account to one time and context, so it does not establish a general causal effect on business outcomes. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1 · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions
- [statement] Citation governance should preserve enough context to assess a decision: Burghardt warns that isolated evidence can be cherry-picked, retention-driven deletion can break evidence links, and even citation patterns do not prevent citing the wrong insights. An insight summary can include both supporting and contradicting evidence, but takes additional preparation effort. (low confidence) — https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance
- [statement] Baymard observed that minor misspellings could remove autocomplete guidance or produce irrelevant suggestions. Correcting spelling only after submission misses users who keep revising in the field or abandon search before submitting; evaluate typo recovery during query entry as well as on the results page. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/offer-autocomplete-suggestions-for-misspellings · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] W3C’s status-message criterion requires displayed status messages to be programmatically determinable so assistive technology can present them without receiving focus. Its guidance cautions against overly chatty announcements and does not require authors to invent additional status messages; test the feedback level with users. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] A Harbor issue records a disagreement about list navigation. The reporter says Back resets page and query; commenter AllForNothing defends refresh as protection against stale repository data. Commenter DuttaNeel07 proposes preserving page and query in the URL while fetching fresh data, with fallback if the saved page disappears. These are attributed reports and proposals, not proof of a shipped fix or current behavior. (low confidence) — https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/issues/23142 · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Keep evidence about AI answers separate from classic result-list search. In NN/G’s exploratory remote study, traditional search and AI chat were used together and sometimes to check each other; nobody relied entirely on generated answers. The study involved nine participants from North America and the UK, so these observations do not establish population prevalence or a universal AI-search replacement effect. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-changing-search-behaviors/ · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Baymard recommends retaining the submitted query in an editable search field: its ecommerce tests found that persistence lets users add or remove words without retyping the full query. It also recommends showing the query on the results page to make the origin of the results clear. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/persist-search-queries · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper describes per-filter application as an intermediate option: users finish searching and selecting within a multi-select dropdown, then apply that filter by closing the dropdown or using its inline Apply action. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper recommends showing active selections in their controls, marking controls containing selections, and providing an applied-filter summary. It recommends clearing selections both within an individual filter and globally. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] The W3C explanation of the status-messages criterion distinguishes a search result list from messages about its progress or completion. Search progress, result-count and no-result messages that update without focus or page refresh should be programmatically available to assistive technology; the result list itself is outside this particular criterion. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Baymard’s ecommerce research says generic search tips alone often leave users stuck. It recommends actionable related-query suggestions, including broadening an overly specific query by removing keywords, to give users a path out of zero results. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/no-results-page · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Baymard recommends that if a zero-results search has only one alternate query, it may be applied automatically with an explicit notice that the original query returned nothing and the displayed results come from the revised search. This is attributed ecommerce guidance, not a universal rule for exact-match or high-stakes search. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/no-results-page · keywords: UI/UX design: longitudinal research, search interaction and ResearchOps, Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] NN/g’s qualitative study used remote usability sessions with nine participants from North America and the UK. All used traditional search multiple times and none relied entirely on generative responses. This finding concerns those sessions; it does not establish population adoption rates or prove that AI answers replace result-list interaction.
